Consequently, the characters of ordinary $L_{-3}(F_4)$-modules satisfy a fifth-order modular linear differential equation. We also give modular linear differential equations of orders five and eleven satisfied by the characters of ordinary modules for $L_{-2}(B_3)$ and $L_{-2}(G_2)$ respectively.

title: AI Information Synthesis and Content Polarization
authors: Chang Liu, Yuting Zhu
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) can synthesize dispersed information into balanced and informative content, raising the possibility that AI may help reduce polarization. We show that this promise can be undermined by the strategic response of content producers. We develop a game-theoretic model in which consumers acquire information to make downstream decisions, content producers allocate limited informational capacity between broadly valuable vertical information and horizontally differentiated information, and AI provides an alternative source of synthesized information. The effects of AI unfold in three phases as its reliability increases. When reliability is low, AI has no effect on the market. At intermediate levels, AI disciplines prices without attracting consumers or changing content. When AI becomes sufficiently reliable, consumers begin to substitute toward it, and content producers respond by shifting informational capacity away from the vertical dimension and toward horizontally differentiated content, thereby increasing content polarization. The mechanism operates through audience composition: AI attracts consumers who are less well matched to individual producers, leaving producers with stronger incentives to cater to their remaining audiences. The polarization effect intensifies with AI reliability but weakens with greater competition among content producers. Our findings highlight a potential wedge between AI's direct and equilibrium effects: a technology that provides consumers with more balanced information can indirectly make the broader content ecosystem more polarized.

title: PrT-Flow: Probability-Tractable Flow Matching for Reinforcement Learning
authors: Congzhong Sun, Ning Tan
abstract: Diffusion models and Flow Matching can represent flexible distributions over robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also require the probability of each action. We introduce PrT-Flow (Probability-Tractable Flow Matching), which computes probability density while retaining multimodal, multi-step action generation. Its Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) makes each sampling step invertible and enables efficient computation of its Jacobian determinant. We train these finite steps with Conditional Euler-step Training (CET), which supervises their displacement over one step during sampling rather than their instantaneous velocity. We prove that, under certain assumptions, CET has the same minimizers as fitting the Euler-solver updates of Flow Matching. PrT-Flow achieves 96% success on Robomimic Lift after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion policy reference, and 96% success on OGBench Cube-Triple after 600k online steps. These results demonstrate that invertible networks with tractable probability densities can learn effective robot policies and support SAC-style actor-critic training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sunlight-zero/PrT-Flow .

title: Decouple to Forget: Semantic Mediation for Sensitive Unlearning in Large Language Models
authors: Jingyue Cong, Andy Song, Yang Yu, Tabinda Sarwar, Xinshu Li, Ziqi Xu, Xun Yi, Ke Wang, Bo Han, Estrid He
abstract: Machine unlearning for large language models seeks to remove specified knowledge while preserving general capability, yet current methods often treat an entire response as the unit of forgetting. This coarse granularity causes unnecessary utility loss when the forget target is only a small set of sensitive facts embedded within otherwise benign explanations. In this paper, we introduce Decouple to Forget (D2F), a targeted unlearning method inspired by semantic mediation that separates sensitive factual content from non-sensitive meaning and surface expression. For each example to be forgotten, D2F extracts a fact-level "mediator" representation from the answer, identifies which parts are sensitive, and removes only those parts while leaving the rest of the structure intact. We then generate counterfactual answers grounded in this mediator that preserve non-sensitive content but exclude sensitive facts, employing preference-based contrastive optimization to reduce the likelihood of information leakage while maintaining helpfulness and fluency. Experiments across various benchmark datasets show that D2F achieves a better balance between forgetting and retention than strong baseline methods. Our code is available at https://github.com/JingyueCong/D2F.

title: New results from electron-positron heavy-flavor factories
authors: Xiaodong Shi
abstract: The electron-positron heavy-flavor factories --- BaBar, Belle, Belle~II, and BESIII --- continue to deliver a broad and sensitive physics program. I report selected highlights presented at ICHEP 2026, covering neutral- and charged-current $B$ processes, tests of lepton-flavor universality in $b\to c\ellν$ transitions, precision measurement of Cabibbo--Kobayashi--Maskawa matrix elements, and hadron spectroscopy.

title: Experimental evidence for physical alteration of fine regolith on near-Sun asteroids
authors: Jooyeon Geem, Mikael Granvik, Georgios Tsirvoulis, Leonard Schirner, Marianna L. Kemell, Antti Penttila, Axel Hagermann, Athanasia Toliou
abstract: The surfaces of airless bodies evolve through processes such as (micro)meteoroid impacts and thermal fatigue, which modify physical properties such as grain size, porosity, and mineral texture. These properties provide clues to surface evolution and are necessary for interpreting telescopic observations. Near-Sun asteroids (NSAs), which reach heliocentric distances of $\lesssim$0.2 au, are notable targets, as their surfaces are likely modified by intense solar radiation. However, experimental studies of how radiative heating modifies the physical properties of carbonaceous asteroid surfaces remain scarce compared with studies of thermally induced compositional and spectral changes. We investigate these modifications experimentally. Near-Sun conditions at heliocentric distances $0.09<r<0.19$ au are simulated using the Space and High-Irradiance Near-Sun Simulator. CM-type carbonaceous chondrite simulants are irradiated under vacuum. Brightness is monitored in situ with a video camera during heating, and morphological changes are examined using a stage microscope and a scanning electron microscope (SEM). The irradiated samples show initial darkening followed by brightening, consolidation, and morphological modifications from sub-micrometer to millimeter scales. The observed brightness modifications are more consistent with changes in the absorption properties of the sample than with variations in surface roughness. SEM imaging of the heated samples shows structures similar to those formed by sintering, which are completely absent in unheated samples. These results suggest that sintering is a likely candidate for the mechanism responsible for the observed consolidation and morphological changes. This work provides experimental evidence to help constrain the surface evolution of NSAs in general, and supports sintering as a possible mechanism proposed for (3200) Phaethon in particular.

title: Code2Worlds-2: Physically Plausible Agent Harness for Embodied World Simulation
authors: Haoyu Zhang, Siming Li, Zeyu Zhang, Yi Zhang, Tat-Seng Chua, Hao Tang
abstract: Recent coding large language models (LLMs) can synthesize dynamic 4D worlds from natural language, but the resulting content remains a visual artifact. It lacks physical semantics such as the collision geometry, mass, friction, inertia, and joint structure, required to enable it to simulate the physical world, and its dynamics are scripted to look plausible rather than designed to execute. What is needed is an executable world: one that a physics engine can load and step, resolving contact physically. We present Code2Worlds-2, an extension of Code2Worlds that turns 4D world generation into an embodied world simulation. We keep the original dual-stream generation pipeline intact and append two modules. First, a SimReady Scene Compiler that turns a generated visual scene into a simulator-compatible representation: it assigns collision meshes via convex decomposition, estimates physical attributes with a vision-language model, infers a lightweight support graph, instantiates the engine's contact, friction, and dynamics constraints, and applies a gravity settling pass, before exporting the scene as MuJoCo MJCF. Second, a Simulator-in-the-Loop 4D Refiner that implements an automated agent harness-a compile, simulate, critique and refine loop-that converts visual dynamics into executable rigid and articulated dynamics and evolves the physical settings rather than only the code, replacing the purely visual motion critic with a simulator critic that inspects penetration depth, collision pairs, stability, contact forces, joint limits, and robot reachability. We further propose SimCode4D, a state-based benchmark with five task templates for evaluating embodied simulation. Experiments on SimCode4D and across natural, indoor, industrial, urban, and service scenes show that Code2Worlds-2 produces physically plausible, simulator-compatible, and robot-interactable scenes.

title: DisaggKD: Efficient Knowledge Distillation through Teacher-Student Disaggregation and a Fused Loss
authors: Ruixuan Tu, Yuyang Dong
abstract: Knowledge distillation (KD) frameworks place teacher and student on the same GPUs, so per-GPU memory limits the teachers that fit. DisaggKD separates them across nodes: teacher replicas stream hidden states to the student, a KD loss over row windows and vocabulary shards equals the full-vocabulary loss in exact arithmetic without forming the full-vocabulary logits, and a prefetch ring paces producer and trainer. Closed-form memory and traffic models locate the memory limits of each layout. On the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B to 9B pair, the disaggregated layout matches the LM loss of the colocated run with the same loss and is faster than that run; our fused loss also lets a colocated run train on as few nodes at faster speed, while the split is memory efficient when the student spans several nodes. On the larger pairs, colocated runs with a fused loss still run OOM where the split trains, because teacher weights and student states fill the budget.

title: The Tokens Strike Back: Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision
authors: Amman Yusuf, Jiwoo Shin, Ruizhi Deng, Heitor Rodrigues Guimarães, Nikita Dvornik, Mijung Park
abstract: The Safety-Aware Denoiser (SAD) is a recent, training-free, safety-guidance framework for text diffusion models. During inference, SAD steers text samples toward safe regions of the token probability space. In this paper, we propose $\mathit{SADDER}$ (Safety-Aware Denoising with Directional Embedding-based Revision), which improves the safety and quality trade-offs of SAD by exploiting a safety-guidance signal in the embedding (or activation) space for each token position, then updating the token positions using the SAD update rule multiplied by the guidance signal. This multiplication acts as a gating mechanism: tokens with a high unsafe signal are more likely to be modified during inference following the SAD update rule. However, such an update does not automatically preserve the conditional mean, i.e., the denoiser of a fixed target distribution. We therefore theoretically derive new position-wise target distributions for which the modified denoiser is exact. Furthermore, we derive conditions under which the position-wise target distributions match a global target distribution. We test our $\mathit{SADDER}$ method on popular Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs) and Uniform-State Diffusion Models (USDMs) across unsafe continuation and jailbreak settings, and show that $\mathit{SADDER}$ achieves a better balance between safety, generation quality, and inference cost than existing methods.

title: Berezin Ranges of Composition Operators on $H^2$
authors: Paul Bourdon, Trieu Le, Derek Thompson
abstract: We explore properties of the Berezin range $B(C_φ)$ of a composition operator $C_φ$ on the Hardy space $H^2$, including constraints on its location in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, topological properties, shape, symmetry, and convexity. For example, we show that $B(C_φ) \subseteq \{z\in \mathbb{C}: \Re(z) > 0 \ \text{and}\ |z| \le 1 + |φ(0)|\}$, that $B(C_φ)$ is closed if and only if $C_φ$ is the identity operator, and that $B(C_φ)$ containa all its boundary points except for $0$ if $C_φ$ is compact. Addressing questions raised by Cowen and Felder, we show that $C_φ$ can be a (nondegenerate) disk and characterize when $B(C_φ)$ is convex if $φ$ is linear.

title: Toward Interpretable Quantum Generators for Financial Returns through Problem-Informed Circuit Design
authors: Huijie Guan, Xuanhao Wang, Shengbin Wang, Jiale Zhang, Jian Ding, Shuxin Xie, Dongdong Li, Jianjian Gao, Hantao Sun, Wenhao Chu
abstract: When used as function approximators, quantum circuits often lack interpretability and face a fundamental trade-off between expressivity and trainability. We propose a problem-informed framework for financial return generation that uses relational structure and symmetry-inspired parameter sharing to guide the construction of quantum circuits with few trainable parameters and empirically testable operator roles. We evaluate three quantum generator architectures, referred to as ZZ, directed ZZ-CRX, and structured time evolution, within a hybrid Wasserstein quantum generative adversarial network trained to generate 16-step Bitcoin return windows. Across circuits with one to four layers and one to eight trainable coefficients, these generators recover meaningful marginal and temporal distributional features, while single-layer configurations remain competitive with deeper variants. Across matched depths, independently trained ZZ-CRX configurations exhibit a predominantly downward shift in median leverage relative to ZZ, consistent with the intended directional role of the controlled-rotation construction. The small number of coefficients also enables direct landscape analysis, revealing competing parameter preferences between marginal and temporal objectives and helping to explain the difficulty of finding parameter settings that perform well on both. These results provide an initial demonstration that structural assumptions can guide the design of compact quantum generators and link circuit architecture to observable statistical behaviour, motivating more systematic and parameter-efficient approaches to quantum circuit construction.

title: Optimal transportation under McKean-Vlasov dynamics
authors: Camilo Hernández, Ludovic Tangpi
abstract: We study a broad class of stochastic transport problems under controlled McKean-Vlasov dynamics, allowing control of both drift and volatility, with weak terminal constraints. In contrast to the classical Schrödinger problem, the reference dynamics depend on the evolving law of the process, leading to nonlinear optimization problems on path space, while the terminal constraint is formulated through weak optimal transport, permitting a flexible treatment of distributional targets. This framework encompasses several problems of current interest, including the mean field Schrödinger problem, martingale optimal transport, and Schrödinger-Bass bridges. We establish three main results. First, we prove the existence of optimal controls under general coercivity, continuity, and convexity assumptions. Second, we derive a convex dual representation that extends weak Kantorovich duality and stochastic optimal transport duality to controlled McKean-Vlasov dynamics. Finally, for the mean field Schrödinger problem, we prove convergence, at the level of value functions, of the associated finite-particle Schrödinger bridge problems to the mean field limit, thereby identifying the nonlinear problem as the exact infinite-particle limit of finite-particle Schrödinger bridges. As a byproduct, we establish the existence of an optimal mean field Schrödinger potential, providing a variational foundation for duality in nonlinear stochastic transport.

title: FedLoRD: Personalized Federated Learning based on Low-Rank Structures of Model Parameter Differences
authors: Tsutahiro Fukuhara, Junya Hara, Hiroshi Higashi, Yuichi Tanaka
abstract: We propose FedLoRD, a personalized federated learning (PFL) method based on the low-rank structure of the differences between the global and personalized model parameters. PFL is a branch of federated learning that aims to learn models tailored to the local data of each client under biased local data distributions. In its local training, each client learns a personalized model by regularizing the difference between its model parameters and the global ones sent from the server. The regularization function needs to be designed with priors on the model parameter difference; however, the existing PFL methods rely on empirical choices (e.g., $\ell_1$- and $\ell_2$-norms), which do not take into account the actual characteristics of the difference. The resulting mismatch of priors can lead to suboptimal personalized models. To address this issue, we propose a PFL method whose regularizer is built on an observed characteristic of the model parameter differences: they are approximately low-rank at every layer. In our method, we first formulate a local training problem with nuclear norm regularization on the layer-wise differences. We further rewrite this problem via the factorized representation of the nuclear norm so that it can be efficiently solved by a plain stochastic gradient descent method. Image classification experiments on three benchmark datasets demonstrate that FedLoRD outperforms several existing PFL methods.

title: Observational evidence of black hole event horizon from ultra-compact X-ray binaries
authors: Qian-Qi Ma, Wei-Min Gu, Shan-Shan Weng, Mouyuan Sun
abstract: The event horizon is the most crucial feature that distinguishes black hole (BH) from all other objects in the universe. However, since no radiation can escape from the event horizon, its direct observational evidence remains lacking. Although both are compact objects, the event horizon leads to differences in the radiative behavior between black hole and neutron star (NS) X-ray binaries. Historically efforts to probe the existence of event horizons revealed that the BH X-ray binaries are fainter than NSs with similar orbital periods in their quiescent states. Here, we use a special class of X-ray binaries namely the ultra-compact X-ray binaries (UCXBs), to reveal the existence of the event horizon near stellar-mass black holes. In short-period UCXBs, gravitational radiation dominates the orbital angular momentum loss, allowing us to accurately determine their accretion rates. Based on five UCXBs with orbital periods shorter than 40 min, located in globular clusters, and identified accretors (NS or BH), we obtained their accretion rates. Combining their accretion rates and X-ray luminosities, we calculated the X-ray radiative efficiencies of NS and BH. The radiative efficiency of BH is about two to three orders of magnitude lower than that of NS systems, indicating the accretion energy is swallowed by the BH, thereby indirectly probe the presence of the event horizon.

title: $3$-manifold groups are linear
authors: Xiaolei Wu, Shengkui Ye
abstract: We prove that the fundamental group of every compact graph $3$-manifold is linear over the complex numbers. As a corollary, all fundamental groups of compact $3$-manifolds are linear over the complex numbers.

title: Constrained Grid-Forming Control for Photovoltaic Systems: A Control Barrier Function Approach
authors: Amir Afshari, Dominic Groß
abstract: This paper leverages control barrier functions (CBFs) to systematically account for constraints of voltage source converters (VSCs) and photovoltaic (PV) resources in grid-forming (GFM) control. The proposed control combines (unconstrained) dual-port GFM control with control barrier functions (CBFs) to ensure reliable and safe operation of a GFM PV system under grid faults, sudden changes in irradiance, and load perturbations. First, CBFs are used to encode physical and operational limits of the PV system, namely current and voltage limits at its ac and dc terminals. Then, CBFs are used to restrict the dynamics of dual-port GFM control to within the VSC and PV limits during both transient and steady states. To this end, a cost function is defined that encodes trade-offs between forming the ac voltage phase angle/frequency and voltage magnitude under constraints. Then, real-time optimization is used to make the least modification, as measured by the cost function, to the (unconstrained) dual-port GFM control state to remain within the safe set encoded by the CBFs. Finally, the performance of the developed constrained GFM control is evaluated through EMT simulations in MATLAB/Simulink.

title: TDR: Tagalog Diacritic Restoration Dataset
authors: Ivan Yuri De Leon, Lanz Railey Fermin, Zachary Aldridge Africa, Richell Isaiah Flores
abstract: Homographs are words that share identical spelling but differ in meaning and pronunciation. In Tagalog, these distinctions are disambiguated in writing through tuldik (diacritical marks), which are rarely preserved in contemporary Tagalog text. This scarcity of diacritics limits diacritic restoration, which is useful for downstream tasks such as prosody selection for text-to-speech synthesis. To address this gap, this study introduces TDR, an annotated corpus of 40 frequent Tagalog homographs constructed from news text. It also introduces a collocation-driven retrieval method to expand the dataset and mitigate severe class imbalance among minor variants. Finally, we show that TDR supplies a capability absent from pretrained models, and that this capability can be learned by small, inexpensive models as well as by fine-tuned LLMs.

title: Revisiting the 16x Pretraining Compute Gap between Diffusion and Autoregressive Language Models
authors: Guanghan Wang, Bing He, Zhan Shi, Benoit Dumoulin, Hanqing Lu, Volodymyr Kuleshov
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) have attracted wide attention for their fast, parallel decoding, but they are believed to be far less efficient to train than autoregressive language models (ARMs): a widely cited study reports that a DLM needs roughly 16x the training compute of an ARM to match its likelihood, a figure that has made pretraining DLMs from scratch look prohibitive at scale. We find that the methodology behind this figure has fallen out of step with current DLM practice: it scores the model with its evidence lower bound (ELBO) and trains a full-sequence, decoder-only model. We therefore revisit the scaling laws of DLMs, adopting the exact likelihood under the model's own decoding order, block diffusion training, an encoder-decoder architecture, and a sweep over the block sizes used in practice. Under this new protocol, we study across ten model variants, about 1,700 models in total, and find that pretraining DLMs is far cheaper than previously thought. Concretely, scoring with the exact likelihood reduces the compute multiple to 12.8x; block diffusion training and an encoder-decoder architecture further reduce it to 7.8x at block size 32, and smaller block sizes narrow it to 4.6x at block size 8 and 3.0x at block size 4. We complement these scaling analyses with an empirical rule for the optimal decoder depth of encoder-decoder block diffusion, a held-out compute budget beyond the fitting range at which the gap between variants persists, and downstream benchmark results where likelihood improvements carry over to accuracy. Overall, the 16x figure substantially overstates the pretraining cost gap between DLMs and ARMs, and pretraining DLMs from scratch is far more viable than previously assumed.

title: Nonhomogeneous Subordinators and Lévy Copulas for Reliability Analysis of Time-Dependent Degradation Processes
authors: Yu Shi, Qianmei Feng
abstract: Many systems in engineering applications may experience complex multi-dimensional degradation processes involving random jumps. Analyzing the reliability of such degradation processes presents significant challenges. Previously developed models have utilized multi-dimensional Lévy subordinators and Lévy copulas to describe these processes, with reliability functions expressed through characteristic functions and Laplace transforms (Shu et al., 2015, 2016, Shi et al., 2020, Shi and Feng, 2024). However, these models are restricted to stationary linear paths and homogeneous Lévy subordinators. In real-world scenarios, increments in a degradation process are often time-dependent and nonhomogeneous. To address this limitation of previous studies, this work extends existing degradation models by introducing nonhomogeneous Lévy subordinators, which are designed to capture time-varying complexities inherent in degradation processes. Unlike conventional degradation models that often assume a constant rate of jumps, nonhomogeneous Lévy subordinators aim to provide a more flexible representation of degradation behaviors that evolve under varying external conditions and internal system dynamics. Additionally, the joint behaviors of multiple degradation processes are characterized using Lévy copulas, enabling a more comprehensive analysis of system reliability. Numerical examples are provided to illustrate the applicability of these models in lifetime analysis.

title: Risk-Averse Inference-Time Diffusion Model Alignment with Finite-Sample Guarantees
authors: Yuchen Liang, Xian Yu
abstract: Inference-time alignment steers diffusion models toward downstream objectives without costly fine-tuning, but existing methods typically optimize expected cost (or reward) without explicitly controlling tail risk. In this work, we propose a risk-averse framework for inference-time alignment of diffusion models that balances expected cost and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CVaR) under trajectory-level Kullback-Leibler regularization. We characterize the optimal path distribution and reverse transitions as functions of the CVaR threshold, reducing the alignment problem to a one-dimensional optimization problem over the threshold. We show that this one-dimensional optimization problem can be nonconvex in general, establish sufficient conditions for convexity, and introduce quadratic regularization to enable efficient derivative-free ternary search. Under suitable assumptions, we provide finite-sample guarantees for threshold optimization and value estimation, and combine them into a terminal total-variation bound relative to the regularized target under exact resampling. Experiments on synthetic data and image generation using Stable Diffusion demonstrate improved tail performance over risk-neutral baselines while maintaining competitive average cost.

title: Benchmarking Self-Supervised 3D Medical Vision Foundation Models and Transferability Estimation
authors: Jiaqi Tang, Yu Wang, Yang Liu, Jing Tao, Fandong Zhang, Zhou Zhen, Xiahai Zhuang, Qingchao Chen, Yining Yang, Yizhou Yu
abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has expanded the pool of 3D medical foundation models, but published evaluations use different datasets, endpoints and fine-tuning protocols. Models also differ in architecture, pretraining objective and data, while downstream targets range from voxel-level masks to patient-level diagnoses and outcomes. As a result, published findings provide little directly comparable evidence for choosing a model for a new task. Direct comparison of adaptation performance requires fine-tuning candidates on labelled target data, at substantial computational cost. We benchmark 23 candidates across the same 14 segmentation, classification and regression tasks spanning multiple anatomies and modalities. No candidate ranked among the top three across all segmentation tasks or across all classification and regression tasks; a convolutional encoder could outperform a transformer trained with the same objective on one task but underperform it on another. We benchmark transferability estimators against the fine-tuned rankings and find that their agreement varies across dense segmentation, classification and regression. InsightRank uses task-appropriate frozen-feature statistics and architecture-aware pairwise comparisons to rank candidates before fine-tuning. Across the 23-model pool, mean Kendall tau-b was 0.431 for segmentation and 0.352 for classification and regression. The segmentation Top 3 contained a task winner on four of nine tasks; the image-level Top 3 contained none on the five tasks, despite better full-ranking agreement than the matched conventional estimators. A three-model shortlist reduced recorded extraction-plus-training job time by 85.8% across seven segmentation tasks. Together, the benchmark provides a common reference for model selection and InsightRank offers a lower-cost way to prioritize fine-tuning, with shortlist performance that differs by target type.

title: Puncturing-inclusion constructions of optimal Ferrers diagram rank-metric codes using semifield codes
authors: Dengming Xu, Chengming Duan, Yong Jin, Yuhao Ning
abstract: Ferrers diagram rank-metric codes are essential components of the multilevel construction of constant dimension codes for random network coding. This paper aims to construct optimal Ferrers diagram rank-metric codes, focusing on the diagram \([3,3,3,5]\) with rank distance \(3\). We construct an optimal \([[3,3,3,5],6,3]_q\) Ferrers diagram rank-metric code for every prime power \(q\), thereby answering an open problem posed by Etzion et al. in 2016~\cite{Etzion2016}. The construction first builds a \([3\times4,4,3]_q\) MRD code and then proves that the Delsarte dual of its puncturing on the last column contains a \([3\times3,3,3]_q\) MRD code, which comes from semifield codes. We further construct optimal Ferrers diagram rank-metric codes for two infinite families of Ferrers diagrams: the first relies on the \([[3,3,3,5],6,3]_q\) construction and holds for every prime power \(q\), while the second is binary and obtained directly by the puncturing-inclusion construction.

title: Mobility-Budget-Constrained Submodular Maximization for Distributed Semantic Multi-Robot Exploration
authors: Changxuan Yao, Sandilya Sai Garimella, Lu Gan, Panagiotis Tsiotras
abstract: Multi-robot exploration under communication and mobility constraints requires balancing information gain with reachability. We present a distributed semantic exploration framework that combines Dirichlet mapping, budget-constrained trajectory selection, and Resource-Aware distributed Greedy (RAG) coordination. Each robot clusters frontiers, computes terrain- and heading-aware least-cost paths with a single budget-limited Dijkstra search, and selects feasible paths by marginal information gain, represented by the expected reduction in Dirichlet entropy. Each robot's per-round selection is exact, the team's joint per-round information gain is at least half the centralized optimum, and the bound degrades gracefully under limited communication. Ten-run gridworld ablations show improved coverage, semantic mIoU, and map certainty with lower entropy and traversal cost per unit distance than shortest-distance frontier selection. Budget-sensitivity experiments show that an intermediate budget best balances path reach and receding-horizon execution. In photorealistic full-system simulation against five coordination rules run in their native published forms, the proposed method attains the highest mean coverage and semantic accuracy while being the only one that respects the per-trajectory mobility budget.

title: A radio counterpart of the local little-red-dot J092359+415736
authors: Tao An, Ruqiu Lin, Ailing Wang
abstract: Little red dots (LRDs) are compact red sources at z>~4. Broad lines suggest accreting black holes, yet radio and X-ray measurements are usually weak. Local LRDs allow multi-frequency, multi-epoch radio studies that are inaccessible at high redshift. We search archival radio images for a counterpart to the local LRD J092359+415736 at z~0.323, quantify its long-term radio variability, and identify the plausible origin of the radio emission. Flux densities at the optical position are measured in FIRST, LoTSS, RACS, VAST, and VLASS products spanning 0.144-3.0 GHz and 1994-2024. A compact 144 MHz counterpart is detected at 42sigma in LoTSS, coincident with the Gaia position, and is recovered in FIRST, RACS, VAST, and VLASS. LoTSS and ASKAP give a spectral index alpha ~ -0.30 +/- 0.11. The source varies on multiple timescales: FIRST at 1.4 GHz (1994) is a factor of ~2.6 below ASKAP (2021-2024) and below the extrapolated LoTSS-ASKAP spectrum, indicating long-term brightening over 26 yr; the 3 GHz flux density rises by 2.3sigma between VLASS epochs 2.2 and 3.2. A star-formation-only origin would require ~200 Msun/yr, against an unobscured H-alpha upper limit of 3.3 Msun/yr, implying an extreme obscured starburst. Ordinary radio supernovae and tidal disruption events are strongly disfavoured by the luminosity and 30-yr recovery, while refractive scintillation would itself require an ultracompact nuclear emitter. The persistent radio counterpart is best explained by accretion onto the central black hole. Among the three radio-detected local LRDs, this source is intermediate in luminosity and the only one with reported multi-year variability, adding a temporal dimension to the radio diversity of the class.

title: ATOM: Abstract Transition and Option Modeling - Experience-Informed Hierarchical Navigation
authors: Changxuan Yao, Panagiotis Tsiotras
abstract: We propose ATOM (Abstract Transition and Option Modeling), a hierarchical navigation framework that combines higher-level graph planning with reusable lower-level option policies for efficient repeated navigation in large-scale 3D environments represented by hierarchical structures such as 3D scene graphs (3DSGs). ATOM operates on a hierarchical graph representation, implemented using, for instance, the Rooms and Places layers of a 3DSG, where each directed abstract transition is associated with a navigation option. For each transition, ATOM computes and stores a reusable option policy along with its state-dependent cost-to-go. Across repeated navigation tasks, ATOM maintains a smoothed empirical distribution over option initiation states and uses it to progressively refine the corresponding abstract transition cost. Ablation studies show that ATOM reduces cumulative repeated-planning time by 97.5% relative to a monolithic MDP baseline while maintaining trajectories within approximately 7% of a Global Places A* shortest-path reference. Experience-informed refinement further reduces abstract transition-cost estimation error by 10.3%. Physical experiments validate ATOM on an F1Tenth vehicle, successfully completing all five navigation queries with 43% of inter-region option executions reusing previously generated solutions.

title: FLAI Protocol: Decentralized Federated Learning with On-Chain Rewards and sPEG-Based Contribution Scoring
authors: Eli Yune, Mahesh Balan
abstract: Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative model training without data centralization but struggles with incentive alignment, accountability, and robustness under heterogeneous non-IID data. Existing decentralized FL (DeFL) systems leverage blockchains for coordination yet face high on-chain overhead, unverifiable self-reports, and weak fairness guarantees. We present the FLAI Protocol, a trusted execution environment (TEE)-backed DeFL framework that integrates enclave-validated aggregation, sparse Peer Evaluation Graph (sPEG) scoring, and on-chain settlement. sPEG incorporates peer-based quality, class coverage, promptness, effort, and reputation into composite contribution scores. The protocol formalizes contribution evaluation and tokenized incentive distribution, ensuring verifiable fairness and resilience against free-riding and collusion. We evaluate FLAI on image, text, and healthcare datasets and demonstrate parity with FedAvg in utility while improving fairness and accountability. A case study in consumer eHealth (aggregating wearable and electronic health record data for real-world evidence generation) illustrates the protocol's applicability to privacy-critical domains where equitable rewards, auditability, and data sovereignty are essential.

title: Many Steps into One: Reasoning Contraction and the Limits of Safe Memory Reuse for LLM Agents
authors: Jianghong Zhou, Hao Rong, Chen Lin, Daoan Zhang
abstract: Thought templates, skill libraries, agent memories and caches turn many reasoning steps into one. We call this reasoning contraction. A contracted memory saves reasoning steps and errors until its facts change, then quietly answers wrong. Most systems trust memories by counting successes and failures. We prove that such counters are badly tuned change detectors: a symmetric counter notices a partial change only after a power of its false-alarm horizon, and an unclipped one may never notice it. On five LLMs answering multi-hop questions over edited facts, ExpeL- and ACE-style counters serve 7.0-13.5x more stale answers than certified memories given the same information, and on code tasks with an exact verifier 35-73x more. Safety also has a price. When facts change and each memory is judged only by its own verified outcomes, one number, the certification load, sets how much reasoning any safe memory can skip, and under Zipf demand it yields a scaling law. Our recipe weighs each memory's failures by its own likelihood ratio, certifies its utility against live reasoning, and restarts the certificate when facts change, with the likelihood-ratio detector as the safety net for unannounced changes; for large edits it also invalidates the memory.

title: Everyone Was Right: Lexical Representations in Language Models Are Both Abstract and Holistic
authors: Zachary Nicholas Houghton, Yu Zhou, Dan Pluth, Vijay K. Gurbani, Vsevolod Kapatsinski
abstract: Lexical representations can encode both abstract information and information specific to particular contexts. We investigate how these forms of information are organized in language models by decomposing contextual word representations into item, class, and word-class interaction components. Across six pretrained transformers and two linguistic categories, we find that the interaction is consistently present, grows across layers, and contains information associated with both item and class. Unlike the nearly orthogonal item and class effects, the interaction overlaps with both and encodes class information beyond the shared class effect. An interaction also emerges in artificial-language learners even when the input contains only additive structure. Together, these findings show that lexical representations combine abstract information with structure specific to particular word-class combinations.

title: Sim4RAD: A MATLAB Toolkit for Design-Phase Sizing, Actuator Selection and URDF-Model Verification of Serial Robotic Arms
authors: Jingchen Li
abstract: Actuator sizing is an early and consequential decision: joint torque and velocity specifications fix the motors, gearboxes and brakes before any CAD model exists. Sim4RAD is a MATLAB toolkit for that phase and for the verification that follows it. It builds a rigid-body model from a handful of parameters, and four analyses supply the specification: a static analysis combining lever-arm sampling with a posture search, giving a rated torque at a chosen payload envelope and a reproducible peak torque; a dynamics pipeline that reshapes a trajectory under one of four constraints, including the actuator torque-speed envelope; a stochastic analysis over many random motions, so a specification rests on a class of motions, not one trajectory; and a workspace and dexterity analysis that separates where the arm can reach from how it can reach there. Replacing the synthesized model by a URDF file turns the same analyses to verification. A 7-DOF anthropomorphic arm is compared in three layouts differing in the shoulder axis order and in whether the last wrist joint is coaxial with the payload. The static demand at half arm length is nearly the same in all three, and it sizes the joints rather than the sampled motion; reordering the shoulder axes leaves the worst-case torque unchanged at 55 N m and the reachable volume within 8 percent. A last wrist joint coaxial with the payload removes its gravity torque, reduces the adjacent wrist joint by almost a third and cuts the last joint demand tenfold in a 5 m/s scan, at the price of dexterity (mean 0.570 to 0.348). The same arm needs 20 to 37 times more torque for a 5 m/s target than for a 2 s motion: the scenario, not the trajectory, must be fixed first. Verification should use the URDF model of the detailed design; the toolkit is available at https://github.com/LasterLi/Sim4RAD.

title: Reconstruction of Interstellar Cosmic Ray Anisotropy via Heliospheric Propagation Modeling and SVD Inversion
authors: Reilly Tom, Paolo Desiati, Juan Carlos Díaz-Vélez, Perri Zilberman
abstract: Ground-based experiments such as the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the High-Altitude Water Cherenkov Gamma-Ray Observatory detect cosmic-ray anisotropy on Earth, but magnetic deflections within the heliosphere complicate interpretation. Understanding the original spatial distribution of cosmic rays in the interstellar medium requires modeling particle propagation across the heliospheric boundary. We constructed a simulated transport model that backtracks antiprotons from Earth to the interstellar medium and maps spatial transfer probabilities across energies using HEALPix representations. Because our transfer matrices are singular, inversion relies on singular value decom- position regularization. Ground-based observations lose the equatorial North-South anisotropy component, severely degrading interstellar map recovery. We developed a geometric circle-fitting algorithm to estimate and reintroduce the missing component into the observed signals. Our results show that restoring the North-South anisotropy en- ables more accurate recovery of the interstellar dipole structure. Furthermore, Poisson statistical fluctuations on the detected event counts dominate matrix-transformation errors when spread over multiple energies.

title: Lifting Finite-Sample Gaussian Approximation of Wide Neural Networks to Functional Convergence
authors: Luis Wiederhold, Nil Ayday, Debarghya Ghoshdastidar
abstract: Randomly initialised neural networks of width $m$ converge to Gaussian processes as $m \to \infty$, with two types of quantitative bounds characterising this convergence. Finite-sample bounds compare the network with its Gaussian limit at a fixed finite sample set, on an arbitrary domain, in the quadratic Wasserstein distance $\mathcal W_2$, achieving a convergence rate of $m^{-1/2}$ with explicit constants. However, these constants grow with the number of samples, so the bound becomes uninformative as the sample set is refined. Functional bounds remove that dependence by comparing the two as random functions, at the price of spherical input, metrics weaker than $\mathcal W_2$, or slower rates. In this paper, we therefore lift a finite-sample bound to a functional one. The lifting refines the sample set until it is dense in the domain, so the bound must first be made independent of the number of samples. We achieve this by measuring the error per sample, which makes the constant uniform. For a polynomial activation and any compact input set, this gives a rate of $m^{-1/2}$ in the supremum norm, with an explicit constant.

title: Simultaneous energy and entropy stability of volume-penalisation immersed-boundary methods for the compressible Navier--Stokes equations
authors: Abbas Ballout, Albert Jiménez-Ramos, Gonzalo Rubio, Esteban Ferrer
abstract: Immersed-boundary methods avoid body-fitted meshes, but the energy or entropy stability of the underlying flow discretisation does not automatically extend to the immersed treatment. This manuscript analyses the volume-penalised compressible Navier--Stokes equations for both energy and entropy stability, on the continuous and semi-discrete levels, and integrates the isolated source exactly in time. The source is formulated as a one-parameter family indexed by $θ$, whose momentum component relaxes the fluid velocity towards the prescribed solid velocity; $θ$ sets how much of the resulting kinetic-energy loss leaves the domain rather than being converted to internal energy. The two stability requirements impose opposing bounds on $θ$, with dissipation of the relative total energy requiring $θ\geq0$ and stability of the mathematical entropy requiring $θ\leq1$. Where penalisation acts, both conditions are therefore satisfied if and only if $0\leqθ\leq1$, and the symmetric value $θ=1/2$ divides the kinetic-energy loss equally between the domain and the internal energy. We conclude that any entropy-stable split-form discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method remains semi-discretely entropy stable once the source is added at the collocation nodes, for stationary and prescribed moving bodies alike.

title: Path Length Existence Problems in Bounded-Treewidth Probabilistic Graphs
authors: Antoine Amarilli, Mikaël Monet, Harshul Sagar
abstract: We consider the problem of computing the probability of existence of a source-to-target path or walk satisfying a given length constraint in an input probabilistic graph. The length constraints we consider can require the length to be at least $\ell$, at most $\ell$, or exactly $\ell$, for $\ell$ a target length given as input. The probabilistic graphs that we consider are directed graphs where each edge is annotated with an independent probability of existence. As this task is generally intractable (#P-hard), we aim for algorithms applying to input graphs that are assumed to be of bounded treewidth. We classify the complexity landscape of these problems: - We give an XP algorithm parameterised by treewidth to compute the probability that an input probabilistic graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length $\geq \ell$, and do the same for a path/walk of length $\leq \ell$. - We show that the four problems mentioned in the last item are W[1]-hard parameterised by pathwidth (hence not FPT under the standard assumption that FPT$\neq$W[1]). This is in contrast to the case of non-probabilistic graphs, where the corresponding problems were known to be FPT parameterised by treewidth; and to the connectivity problem (and more generally MSO evaluation) on probabilistic graphs, where the same was known. - Surprisingly, we show that it is #P-hard to compute the probability that an input graph contains a source-to-target path/walk of length exactly $\ell$, even on graphs of pathwidth $2$. By contrast, all our problems are tractable on graphs of treewidth $1$. - Last, we investigate the complexity of our problems when the edges can carry weights. This causes all our problems to become #P-hard already on pathwidth-2 graphs, and causes specifically the ``exactly $\ell$'' walk problem to be #P-hard even on pathwidth-1 graphs.

title: Bipartite Matching with Few Rounds of Demand Queries
authors: Shravan Mehra, Sagnik Mukhopadhyay, Vihan Shah
abstract: We study the randomised and deterministic demand-query complexity of approximate bipartite matching with few query rounds. The demand-query model, introduced in [Blumrosen and Nisan SICOMP 2009; Nisan SODA 2021], is inspired by combinatorial auctions and welfare maximisation, where an oracle returns the first neighbouring vertex (item) of a vertex u (agent) according to a given permutation pi (preference ordering of the agent over the items). For randomised algorithms, our main result gives a trade-off between the number of rounds k, the per-round query budget q=n^{1+δ}, and the achievable approximation ratio. Let 1 <= k <= log n, and -1 <= delta <= 1/k. Every k-round randomised algorithm using O(q) demand queries per round has a worst-case expected-size approximation factor of Omega(n^{1/2k-delta/2}/k). Conversely, we give a randomised algorithm achieving approximation factor O(n^{(1-k*delta)/(k+1)}/k) in expectation. For deterministic algorithms, for k*q >= n, we show that the optimal deterministic approximation factor is ~Theta(n^2/(q*k^2)), thereby improving the previous lower bound of [Nisan SODA 2021] by a polynomial factor over a wide range of parameters. In particular, for q=Theta(n), we improve the deterministic round-complexity lower bound for constant-factor approximation from ~Omega(n^{1/3}) to ~Omega(sqrt n). Our algorithms produce matching and vertex-cover certificates; the deterministic trade-off also extends to minimum vertex cover and maximum fractional matching. We extend the randomised upper bounds to the weaker Demand-OR model [Nisan 2021]. We prove a non-adaptive simulation of uniform random-neighbour queries using known techniques, avoiding the O(log n)-round penalty of the trivial binary-search simulation. Consequently, our upper bounds yield the same k-round approximation guarantees using O(q * log^2 n) Demand-OR queries per round.

title: PULSUS: Direct Frequency-Domain Multidimensional Spectroscopy Beyond the Impulsive Rotating-Wave Approximation
authors: Alfonso Castillo-Gonzolez, Eric R. Bittnre
abstract: We introduce PULSUS, a direct frequency-domain framework for multidimensional spectroscopy of open quantum systems beyond the impulsive rotating-wave approximation. Coherence-frequency intervals are represented through Liouvillian resolvents, while finite Gaussian pulses are incorporated through operator-valued functions of the field-free Liouvillian. This enables direct evaluation on Cartesian grids or arbitrary spectral coordinates while retaining molecular evolution during the pulse envelopes and, when required, the complete light--matter interaction. The implementation is validated against analytical and independent time-domain benchmarks and supports targeted spectral sampling that reduces the number of evaluated coordinates when the response is spectrally localized. A controlled hierarchy of finite-pulse, rotating-wave, short-pulse, and impulsive models separates the errors introduced by each approximation. For a coupled electronic dimer, the total impulsive-RWA error is nonmonotonic in pulse duration: an intermediate regime provides the highest accuracy, whereas ultrashort pulses expose coupling-enabled beyond-RWA pathways and longer pulses develop substantial finite-pulse corrections. These results show that the impulsive and rotating-wave approximations cannot be assumed to improve simultaneously and should be tested when quantitatively interpreting multidimensional spectra. PULSUS provides a direct frequency-domain framework for carrying out that comparison.

title: Multiboson production at multi-TeV lepton colliders as complementary probes to rare Higgs decays
authors: Dario Buttazzo, Keshav Chaudhary, Roberto Franceschini, Arman Korajac
abstract: We study the potential of very high-energy lepton colliders to probe effective operators affecting the loop-induced Higgs boson decays $h\to γγ$ and $h\to Zγ$, providing constraints complementary to Higgs coupling measurements at the Large Hadron Collider. In particular, we consider processes with two and three bosons in the final state and analyze their individual and combined impact on the effective field theory parameter space. We demonstrate that these processes at a multi-TeV lepton collider can improve the bounds from rare Higgs decays and electroweak precision observables, surpassing the projections for High-Luminosity LHC and FCC-ee. This is especially true for triboson processes, whose sensitivity is enhanced by the growth with energy of the new physics cross-sections, making them the dominant constraint at very high energies, potentially competitive with FCC-hh.

title: $T$-efficient unitary synthesis via block-sparse Hamiltonian simulation
authors: Diyi Liu, Shuchen Zhu, Wibe Albert de Jong, Di Fang, David Williams-Young, Chao Yang
abstract: We construct Clifford+$T$ circuits implementing arbitrary $n$-qubit unitaries with worst-case $T$-count $\widetilde{O}(N^{8/7})$ at constant operator-norm error, where $N=2^n$, improving the previous exponent $5/4$. The construction uses $\widetilde{O}(N^{6/7})$ clean ancillas. The main idea is to reduce the data addressed by each query to the block-encoding circuit for a sparse piece while controlling the additional simulation work needed to combine the pieces. We simulate a Hermitian logarithm of the target by flattening its traceless part with a two-layer random similarity transformation, randomly partitioning the transformed generator into block-sparse Hermitian pieces, and combining their evolutions using qDRIFT. For a target operator-norm error $ε\in(0,1/2)$, let $L=\log_2(N/ε)$, the qubit count plus the requested bits of accuracy. By successively correcting the approximation error, we obtain a circuit using $\widetilde{O}(N^{8/7}L^{3/7}+NL)$ $T$ gates and $\widetilde{O}(N)$ clean ancillas whenever $L\le N$. We also prove that, at constant precision, the exponent $8/7$ is optimal within a sequential block-SELECT model.

title: Gaussian entanglement and quantum communication: geodesic optimization and multimode bounds
authors: Hemant K. Mishra, Mark M. Wilde
abstract: Loss and noise limit the use of light to distribute entanglement, transmit quantum information, and establish secret keys. Gaussian states have a compact description in terms of means and covariance matrices, but their entanglement still requires global optimization. We develop a framework for computing Gaussian-restricted versions of the relative entropy of entanglement and Rains entanglement. An integral representation reveals a convex geometry under matrix geometric means and reduces Gaussian Rains entanglement to relative entropy minimized over Gaussian states with positive partial transpose. We obtain unique optimal reference states and additivity for independent Gaussian input states. Our convex-majorization algorithm has an explicit geometric convergence rate, uniform in the faithful regularization parameter and valid for pure input states. Controlled numerical integration and approximate convex subproblem solutions give a bit-complexity bound that is polynomial in accuracy bits for each fixed rational input covariance matrix, with explicit dependence on covariance size. These calculations bound extractable entanglement and, through the relative entropy of entanglement, extractable secret key. Teleportation simulation, energy allocation, and a convex optimization of passive-basis loss cores give bounds on quantum and private communication under an input-energy constraint, allowing arbitrary two-way classically assisted protocols. Two- and three-mode examples compare the bounds with achievable rates, including matching pure-loss benchmarks. Finally, we separate the Gaussian-restricted quantities from their unrestricted counterparts and give a photon-number truncation method with controlled error for computing the latter.

title: Do Factuality Methods Make LLMs More Factual? Reproducibility and Fair Comparison
authors: Pratuat Amatya, Vinay Setty, V Venktesh, Avishek Anand
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are aligned to human preferences, after pre-training and supervised fine-tuning steps. However, standard RL alignment steps such as RLHF do not focus on factuality of LLMs, hence they may generate non-factual information, which could result in unintended consequences. In response, a number of factuality alignment approaches have been proposed in the literature which claim to improve factuality of LLMs on their own benchmarks. However, these methods have not been reproduced independently and are also not comparable since each uses a different base model, training data, evaluation set, judge, and metric. In this paper, we present the first independent reproduction of five factuality alignment methods, which span on-policy RL (PPO, GRPO, and Dr.~GRPO) and offline preference optimization (DPO and KTO), and compare them on a common benchmark with common evaluation metrics. We found that none of these methods reproduces in full, and on the common benchmark none of the methods significantly outperforms the base model. On closer inspection, the rewards optimize for format, length, or brevity rather than factuality and relevance, whereas the choice between on-policy and offline training matters little. Furthermore, the evaluation metrics and benchmarks are also part of the problem since they do not measure relevance of text to the prompt. Since there is no ground truth associated with the prompts, the reliance on LLM judges and retrieval for verification also makes the evaluation fragile. We release our code, data, and checkpoints.

title: Training Generalist Navigation Policies via Action Self-Distillation
authors: Bowen Feng, Keqin Wang, Yulong Yang, Amogh Joshi, Christine Allen-Blanchette, Dhruv Shah, Felix Heide
abstract: Language provides a natural interface for humans to specify and reason about goals, but training language-conditioned robotic policies and reasoning typically requires expensive manual annotations. We propose Action Self-Distillation (ASD), a method for learning language-conditioned reasoning for robotic navigation without human-annotated language or reasoning labels. ASD uses an open-source VLM, which contains broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, as both a teacher network and a student policy. During training, the self-teacher receives privileged trajectory feedback and infers the underlying navigation goal together with goal-oriented reasoning. The student is then trained to condition on the inferred navigation goal, predict future ego-frame trajectory, and provide a description of the scene semantics, plan, and reasoning, from onboard observations alone. Across 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks, our method improves success rate over the strongest baseline by $30\%$ in indoor settings, $30\%$ on multi-stage tasks, and achieves $95\%$ success rate on outdoor tasks, validating that privileged trajectory feedback can enable self-distillation for scalable generalist navigation policies without human annotations.

title: Wendt's determinant and finiteness of prime characteristics for permutation binomials
authors: Zhichao Tang, Xiang Fan
abstract: For $f(X)=X^r(X^s+a)\in\mathbb F_{p^m}[X]$, with $m,r,s\geqslant1$ and $a\in\mathbb F_{p^m}^\times$, put $g=\gcd(s,p^m-1)$. We prove that, for each fixed $g$, only finitely many prime characteristics $p$ admit such permutation binomials, even as $m,r,s,a$ vary. If $6\nmid g$, every such $p$ divides Wendt's determinant $W_g=\operatorname{Res}_X(X^g-1,(X+1)^g-1)$, which is nonzero. When $6\mid g$, this determinant vanishes; inverse power sums and iterated resultants yield an explicit nonzero integer divisible by every such $p>2g+1$. We determine the exact admissible characteristics for $1\leqslant g\leqslant10$, obtain a further divisibility condition over prime fields, and show that in prime fields $g=11$ occurs precisely when $p=23$.

title: Extensions of Operator Systems, Hyperrigidity and Quantum Double Suspension
authors: Vibhor Bhatt, Satyajit Guin, Palash Sharma
abstract: We introduce a class of extensions of unital operator systems satisfying a certain Toeplitz type property. We show that these extensions induce corresponding extensions of the $C^*$-algebras they generate. We prove that hyperrigidity is preserved under these extensions, yielding new examples through iteration. We introduce the quantum double suspension of operator systems as a special class of these extensions and show that its iterates yield the Hong-Szymański quantum double suspensions at the $C^*$-algebra level, encompassing, in particular, the Vaksman-Soibelman quantum spheres. We construct hyperrigid operator systems underlying these quantum spheres. As a further application, we show that every counterexample to Arveson's hyperrigidity conjecture gives rise to a sequence of counterexamples. We identify the $C^*$-envelopes of these extensions and use this identification to obtain a $K$-theoretic condition ensuring that each such sequence contains infinitely many pairwise non-isomorphic counterexamples. We also observe that the validity of the conjecture in the commutative setting is linked to its validity for an infinite family of noncommutative operator systems obtained through successive extensions. Finally, we compute the propagation number, an invariant of operator systems introduced by Connes and van Suijlekom, for these extensions.

title: ST-GRU PredRNN-V2: A GRU-Based Reformulation of PredRNN-V2 for Video Prediction
authors: Augusta van Haren, Hanna Hoogen, Luca Pattavina, Quincy Rommen
abstract: Video prediction requires models to capture complex spatiotemporal dependencies and to retain relevant information over long sequences. PredRNN and its successor PredRNN-V2 address this challenge with spatiotemporal Long Short-Term Memory (ST-LSTM) units that maintain two separate memory states, at the cost of a relatively complex recurrent building block. In this work, we investigate whether the simpler gating of Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) can be transferred to spatiotemporal predictive learning. To this end, we develop a spatiotemporal GRU (ST-GRU) unit as a GRU-based alternative to the ST-LSTM. The ST-GRU replaces the ST-LSTM's three gates per memory state with two GRU-style gates (update and reset), and merges the temporal memory state into the hidden state, which reduces the number of parameters by about 5%. We incorporate the ST-GRU into PredRNN-V2 and evaluate the resulting model on the Moving MNIST video prediction benchmark, following the original experimental protocol. Averaged over ten predicted frames, the ST-GRU-based PredRNN-V2 achieves an MSE of 55.1, an SSIM of 0.883, an LPIPS of 0.065 and a PSNR of 19.53dB. It does not surpass the original ST-LSTM-based PredRNN-V2 on MSE, SSIM or PSNR, but it achieves a lower LPIPS and performs on par with the earlier ST-LSTM-based PredRNN, while using a simpler recurrent cell. These results suggest that ST-GRUs are a promising building block for spatiotemporal predictive learning and motivate further work on their design and integration.

title: Can the system dynamics remain structurally non-Markovian while its experimentally accessible memory signatures disappear?
authors: Sayan Sengupta, Anish Sharma, George Biswas, Anindya Biswas
abstract: We investigate how unresolved quasistatic disorder in system bath coupling affects non-Markovian dynamics in spin environments. The coupling is fixed within each experimental shot but varies between shots, so repeated shot tomography reconstructs a disorder averaged dynamical map. For a single spin bath with pure dephasing Ising interaction, disorder can drive a transition to CP-divisible dynamics for fixed bath preparations, with a critical strength set by bath polarization along the interaction axis. However, when the bath state fluctuates physically between shots, the averaged dynamics remain CP indivisible at any finite disorder strength. We extend these results analytically to inhomogeneously coupled pure dephasing baths of any number \(N\) of non-interacting spins. At any finite disorder strength, one unpolarized bath spin suffices to retain CP-indivisible dynamics, whereas a fully polarized bath yields Markovian (CP-divisible) dynamics. Dynamics with physically fluctuating bath states likewise remain non-Markovian (CP indivisible) at finite disorder for arbitrary \(N\) in the pure dephasing case. For anisotropic Heisenberg interactions, any nonzero transverse exchange eliminates the disorder driven transition to CP divisibility in a single spin bath. Exact diagonalization of anisotropic models with inhomogeneous couplings up to \(N=12\) reveals persistent trace distance revivals for fixed bath preparations, sampled Haar random preparations, and physically fluctuating bath states, showing that this effect of transverse exchange extends beyond a single bath spin. Increasing disorder still suppresses experimentally accessible revivals and can make memory effects unresolvable at finite measurement resolution even as the dynamics remain CP indivisible. Thus, transverse exchange and physical bath state fluctuations preserve dynamical indivisibility against unresolved coupling disorder.

title: Separating components of real algebraic varieties by cohomological invariants
authors: Olivier Benoist, Samuel Lerbet
abstract: Let $X$ be a smooth algebraic variety over $\mathbb{R}$. We study the separation of the connected components of $X(\mathbb{R})$ by equivariant cohomology, unramified cohomology, and signatures of unramified quadratic forms. Our results highlight how the geometry of $X$ influences these questions. We apply them to cubic hypersurfaces, complete intersections of two quadrics, abelian varieties, and Enriques surfaces. We also obtain new bounds on the exponent of the cokernel of higher signature morphisms in $\mathbf{I}$-cohomology and investigate the optimality of these bounds for smooth projective varieties.

title: Kairos: Transactional Security Enforcement at the System Boundary for LLM Agents
authors: Kristoffer Hempel, Nils Loose, Lorenzo Cavallaro, Thomas Eisenbarth
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents are becoming an integral part of the software development lifecycle, and the capabilities granted to them allow an agent to act with the user's authority on any resource it can access. The reach that gives an agent its utility is equally available to an attacker who can steer it. Anything an agent ingests can carry an injected instruction, and since the model does not reliably distinguish instructions from data, indirect prompt injection should be mitigated by mediating the effects the agent produces. Such mediation faces a structural difficulty. Legitimate work and the first step of an attack often look alike when an individual action is observed, and what separates them lies later in the trace, so a monitor limited to allow and deny is forced to decide before the evidence accumulates. We present Kairos, a reference monitor at the isolation boundary of an unmodified, opaque agent, where a tool call, a shell command, and a script the agent writes all cross the boundary as the same file and network operations, so that confinement holds regardless of the agent's behavior. A declarative policy that states which sources are trusted decides most effects deterministically and defers the rest, which are held while the agent continues speculatively. A decision oracle with bounded authority, such as a language model or a human, releases or refuses each deferred effect on the trace. Across three benchmarks and three agent models, Kairos outperforms existing defenses in the trade-off between attack success and utility. In particular, on AgentDojo, it reduces attack success from 47.0\% to 2.7\% while its benign utility stays at the level of the undefended agent.

title: Traditional and Recent Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 1)
authors: Thierry Bouwmans, Anastasia Zakharova, Belmar Garcia, Marwa Chendeb El Rai, Meghna Kapoor, Badri Narayan Subudhi
abstract: Infrared small target detection is often used in different civilian and military applications to detect static or moving targets in scenes like in ground, air and sea surveillance. First valuable research has emerged since 30 years ago and the two last decades witnessed very significant publications in this field following the rise of low-rank and sparse decomposition (model-based methods) and deep learning models (data-based methods). Furthermore, several surveys can be found in the literature but none of them addresses an overall review in this field. In this context, the aim of this paper is to provide a complete survey of the traditional and recent approaches in infrared small target detection. First, we categorize the different approaches found in the literature in terms of the modeling models, i.e mathematical models, machine learning models and signal processing models. Then, we have discussed them in terms of the critical situations that they claim to handle. Furthermore, we present the available resources, datasets and libraries. Then, we conclude with several promising directions for future research. For the sake of reading, this survey is divided into two parts: 1) "Traditional and Recent Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 1)" about conventional and low-rank and sparse decomposition (model-based methods), and 2) "Traditional and Recent Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 2)" about deep learning models (data-based methods).

title: A CaLLM Judge is a Better Judge: Mitigating Bias in LLM-as-a-judge
authors: Cesare Barbera, Luca Stradiotti, Lorenzo Cascioli, Lorenzo Perini, Niek Tax, Daniel Haimovich, Jesse Davis, Andrea Passerini, Andrea Pugnana
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges to predict which of two candidate answers a human evaluator would prefer, providing a scalable alternative when human evaluation is too costly. Unfortunately, LLM judgments can exhibit systematic biases. Prior work has documented position, verbosity or model family of the candidate answers influencing the judge decision rather than their quality, while additional biases may remain undocumented. $\textit{Multicalibration}$ provides a natural framework to address this problem: each bias corresponds to miscalibration on an identifiable group, $\textit{e.g.}$, family bias manifests as overconfidence in answers generated by models belonging to the same family of the judge. The challenge is to fix miscalibration simultaneously across many, potentially unknown groups. To this end, we introduce $\mathrm{CaLLM}$, a post hoc framework that multicalibrates an LLM judge, thereby bounding all such biases simultaneously. We prove that $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ bounds the bias of every group whose error structure is captured by an available representation, and that augmenting it with explicit bias groups further reduces the residual bias. We then derive theoretical conditions under which $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ improves the judge's accuracy, rather than trading it for calibration. Finally, we evaluate $\mathrm{CaLLM}$ across pairwise preference benchmarks, showing that it reduces the multicalibration error on both specified and unspecified bias groups, while improving predictive performance of the judge.

title: Pseudo-spectral methods in gravitational lensing: Spin precession in loop quantum black hole spacetimes
authors: Xiankai Pang, Xiao-Kan Guo
abstract: Gravitational lensing is usually treated as an initial value problem: for a given impact parameter of an unbound orbit, one computes the resulting deflection angle. In this paper we advocate the inverse point of view. For a prescribed deflection angle, the orbit is selected by two boundary conditions at spatial infinity, so that the lensing problem becomes a well-defined two-point boundary value problem, with the impact parameter playing the role of a nonlinear eigenvalue. We show that pseudo-spectral methods based on Chebyshev collocation solve this boundary value problem accurately at modest computational cost, and that the parallel transport equations governing the spin precession of the particle reduce to a single linear system on the same grid. As a concrete application, we compute the spin precession of massive particles in backward scattering off two black hole spacetimes from loop quantum gravity: the covariant effective metric and the self-dual loop quantum black hole. All equations are written for a general static, spherically symmetric line element with three free functions, so that both spacetimes are handled on the same footing. We find that the quantum corrections are most pronounced for slowly moving particles, while in the ultra-relativistic limit the universal spin flip is always recovered. The flip itself is universal, but the rate at which it is approached is not: the derivative of $\cosξ$ with respect to the particle speed at $v=1$ is a strong-field quantity in every backward channel and depends clearly on the quantum parameters of both spacetimes. The framework is not restricted to the models studied

title: Geometric and homological interpretations of tensor flattenings
authors: Matěj Doležálek, Jakub Jagiełła, Piotr Oszer, Tim Seynnaeve, Colin Stastny
abstract: We relate several nonlinear flattenings of structure tensors of finite algebras and modules to their algebraic and homological invariants. Since smoothability of algebras is equivalent to their structure tensors having minimal border rank, this shows equivalence of several tensor-theoretic nonsmoothability certificates to known classical ones. Particularly, we prove two conjectures of Doležálek and Michałek relating the tangency flattening and the $3\times3$ minor flattening to dimensions of tangent spaces to the Hilbert scheme of points. In the process, we generalize the tangency flattening to a mixed regime with two tensor inputs, relating this to dimensions of $\operatorname{Ext}$ modules, and introduce the dual notion of the cotangency flattening, related to dimensions of $\operatorname{Tor}$ modules. In the case of algebras, we also realize the kernel of the dualized tangency flattening within the setting of Harrison cohomology, making the connection to the tangent space of the Hilbert scheme explicit.

title: Exact Topological Compliance: Generating Persistence-Equivalent Graphs
authors: Mattie Ji, Indradyumna Roy, Vikas Garg
abstract: Persistent homology summarizes the topological evolution of a graph as persistence diagrams (PDs). Generating graphs whose topology matches a target descriptor is increasingly important, yet existing topology-aware generative models rely on soft regularization, producing graphs whose PDs may only be approximately similar. We initiate a principled investigation of the generation problem: produce graphs that realize a target PD exactly. We propose two approaches guided by the implicit local and global constraints a target PD imposes. The local approach builds degree-based PD-equivalent graphs iteratively, and we prove that every output realizes the target PD and that every degree-based PD-equivalent graph is reachable. However, as shown thereafter, local generation necessarily trades off between sample diversity and reaching infeasible states. We therefore recast generation as a global constraint satisfaction problem with a complete encoding solvable by modern constraint programming solvers. This is applicable to any vertex-based permutation equivariant filtration scheme and is minimal under the degree filtration. Experiments on four standard graph generation benchmarks confirm that both methods realize the target PD exactly. Together, our methods provide a principled treatment of strict topology-compliant graph generation. Code is available at https://github.com/Aalto-QuML/ExactCompliance.

title: Cosmic Evolution Survey: LOFAR 144 MHz imaging of the COSMOS field
authors: E. Vardoulaki, T. Shimwell, M. J. Hardcastle, L. Doukas, L. K. Morabito, C. L. Hale, M. T. Sargent, V. Smolčić, G. Zamorani, G. Gozaliasl, F. An, M. Aravena, A. L. Faisst, M. Vaccari, E. Treister, A. Finoguenov, P. Best, J. S. Kartaltepe, C. Casey, S. Jin, V. Mainieri
abstract: We present the first deep, targeted LOFAR 144 MHz source catalogue of the COSMOS field, together with the first 144 MHz source counts in this field. The data comprise 48 h of observations. Over the 2.6 sq. deg. region adopted for the catalogue analysis, the final Dutch-array image reaches a median rms sensitivity of ~100 uJy/beam at an angular resolution of 15" x 6". The resulting catalogue contains 1984 radio sources; a peak S/N >= 5 selection is adopted for the resolved/unresolved classification and source-count analysis. We characterised the catalogue using Monte Carlo source-injection and recovery simulations, including dedicated simulations of extended sources, to quantify completeness, flux-density redistribution, and morphology-dependent source-recovery effects. The catalogue reaches 90% completeness at 1.48 mJy. The resulting Euclidean-normalised differential source counts are measured down to ~0.4 mJy and show good agreement with LoTSS DR3 144 MHz source counts and with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz counts scaled to 144 MHz, with ~5% of catalogue sources having multiple 3 GHz counterparts within a beam-matched search region. Comparison with the VLA-COSMOS 3 GHz catalogue shows good astrometric agreement, with median offsets of Delta_RA = 0.35" (+0.03"/-0.05") and Delta_Dec = -0.83" (+0.02"/-0.03"), approximately 6% of the corresponding synthesised-beam dimensions, and no significant radial dependence across the field. The resulting catalogue provides a low-frequency view of COSMOS and a reference dataset for future deeper LOFAR observations and multiwavelength studies of this extensively characterised extragalactic field.

title: Saturation and semisaturation of oriented graphs
authors: Vladimir Bošković, Balázs Keszegh
abstract: We consider a natural extension of the classical saturation problem to oriented graphs, defined as the minimum number of edges in an oriented graph $H$ on $n$ vertices that avoids a fixed oriented graph $G$, but adding any missing edge to $H$ creates a copy of $G$. Our main result shows that saturation functions of oriented graphs attain at least four distinct orders of magnitude. In particular, if $G$ is acyclic, then its saturation function is bounded if and only if $G$ contains an isolated edge; otherwise, it is linear. Certain tournaments together with an isolated edge give further infinite examples of bounded and linear saturation functions. Two additional orders of magnitude are $Θ(n \sqrt{\log n})$ and $Θ(n \log n)$. For these two, the lower bounds are obtained by adapting a recently developed approach for the saturation problem in edge-ordered graphs, while the matching upper bounds are constructive. Finally, we study the semisaturation problem, in which we require only that adding any missing edge to $H$ creates a copy of $G$. We completely characterize the possible orders of magnitude: the semisaturation function is either bounded, linear, or $Θ(n \log n)$.

title: Some applications of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis to class groups and small generators of number fields
authors: Christopher Frei, Efthymios Sofos, Martin Widmer
abstract: We prove an effective version of the Chebotarev density theorem, conditional on the quasi-Riemann hypothesis for the Dedekind zeta function. Drawing on recent breakthroughs of OpenAI and Cureton--Thorner, we make unconditional the Ellenberg--Venkatesh bounds on $\ell$-torsion in class groups of number fields and extend an averaged result of Lemke Oliver--Smith to arbitrary families of degree-$d$-fields.
