Further, we introduce a transcendental invariant whose sign determines whether exceptional zeros of $S_{2n}(x;χ,χ)$ occur in all sufficiently large degrees, and show that these zeros converge to transcendental limits off the unit circle. For primitive odd characters, we relate this invariant and these limits to Fekete polynomials.

title: Non-additive symmetric rank-metric codes
authors: Marta Messia, Ferdinando Zullo
abstract: We study non-additive rank-metric codes contained in the space of symmetric matrices over a finite field. Our main focus is on symmetric $2$-codes. For odd $q$, we introduce a quotient construction for $\mathrm{Sym}_3(q)$ in which rank-one differences are described by isotropic vectors of a nondegenerate quadratic form on $\mathbb F_q^4$. This leads to a correspondence with partial ovoids of the elliptic quadric $Q^-(5,q)$. Using a construction of Cossidente and Pavese, we obtain a non-additive symmetric $2$-code in $\mathrm{Sym}_3(q)$ of cardinality $q^4+2q^3$, improving the previously known general lower bound. We also give an explicit matrix description of this family. Lastly, we present a block-based construction for symmetric $2$-codes that extends the three-dimensional improvement to all odd dimensions. In particular, for every odd $n\geq3$ and every prime power $q>2$, we obtain \begin{equation*} A_q^{\rm sym}(n,2) \ge q^{(n^2-1)/2}+q^{(n^2-3)/2}+q^{(n^2-9)/2}, \end{equation*} which is strictly larger than the maximum cardinality of an additive symmetric $2$-code with the same parameters. This yields the first infinite family (as the matrix dimension $n$ varies) of non-additive symmetric $2$-codes whose size is larger than the largest achievable size of an additive code with the same parameters; before this, such a gap had only been established for $n=3$.

title: LADDER: A Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation Benchmark
authors: Petko Petkov, Giuliano Albanese, Nikolay Nikolov, Luc Van Gool, Jonathan Tremblay, Danda Pani Paudel
abstract: General-purpose robot manipulation policies learn short-horizon skills effectively, but degrade rapidly on long-horizon tasks. Existing benchmarks cannot isolate failures because task horizon is either too short or entangled with scene and object variations. We propose LADDER, a long-horizon robot manipulation benchmark scaling from 1 to 10 subgoals within the same environment over three suites (SimplerEnv-Long, RobotArena-$\infty$-Long, and RoboLab-Long), 145 tasks, eight categories, two embodiments, and 2,024 simulated episodes per system. We evaluate two orchestration paradigms: text subgoals for learned low-level policies (VoLo) and tool selection orchestration (CaP-X, GPT-Policy, PSP-Agent, TiPToP). Given the full instruction directly, low-level policies achieve 85.4% on single-subgoal tasks, but drop to near zero on extended tasks. While orchestration remedies this, it remains bounded by physical execution errors of the low-level policy rather than high-level planning and achieves only ~25%. Tool selection orchestration with GPT-Policy on GPT-6 Astra significantly outperforms learned-policy methods, but incurs significant time and cost budget and succeeds only ~62%. Real-world experiments across two embodiments confirm the collapse of the low-level policy and the gain from orchestration. Project website: https://ladder.insait.ai

title: Scaling Vision Transformers Without Training: Prune-and-Merge Token Compression
authors: Vatsal, Soumil Malhotra, Priyanshu Chahal, Sanjeev Kumar
abstract: Vision Transformers achieve strong performance but incur high computational costs from quadratic token interactions. Training-free token reduction methods improve efficiency, but their robustness remains underexplored. We propose Prune-and Merge ViT, a training-free framework for off-the-shelf models. It combines class attention-based pruning with similarity-based merging to reduce redundancy while preserving semantic information. To evaluate robustness we introduce two metrics. Relative Accuracy Drop (RAD) measures relative accuracy degradation under transformations, and Prediction Flip Rate (PFR) quantifies prediction consistency. On pretrained ViT and DeiT, Prune-and-Merge reduces computation competitively while maintaining robustness and better accuracy than existing token reduction methods. Our analysis suggests that hybrid token reduction does not introduce hallucination-like behavior and preserves prediction stability for common image transformations.

title: Lifted Restricted Isometry Property and Fast Algorithm for Spectral Compressed Sensing With Near-Optimal Sample Complexity
authors: Xunmeng Wu, Jian-Feng Cai, Zongben Xu, Zai Yang
abstract: This paper studies the spectral compressed sensing problem, which aims to recover an $r$-spectrally-sparse signal of length $N$ from linear compressive measurements. We reformulate the problem as the recovery of a low-rank Hankel matrix. Motivated by this formulation, we propose a Lifted Restricted Isometry Property (LRIP) for the measurement matrix and show that Gaussian measurement matrices satisfy LRIP under certain conditions. Unlike classical RIP, LRIP imposes a rank constraint in the lifted matrix domain while taking measurements in the signal domain through the adjoint Hankel operator. To solve the resulting nonconvex problem efficiently, we introduce a Fast Iterative Hard Thresholding (FIHT) algorithm. Based on LRIP, we show that FIHT converges linearly to the true signal with high probability using $\mathcal{O}(r \ln r \ln^2 N)$ scaled Gaussian measurements, which is near-optimal up to log factors and improves the state-of-the-art order of $r^2$ for nonconvex Hankel methods. Extensive numerical results demonstrate the superiority of FIHT as compared to state-of-the-art convex methods in terms of phase transitions, computational time, and robustness to noise.

title: Box-WAM: Box Trajectories as Compact State Representations for World Action Models
authors: Qinxi Yu, Wenzhou Ding, Gloria X. Wang, Albert J. Zhai, Shenlong Wang
abstract: World action models (WAMs) are a category of policy models that ex- plicitly predict both actions and future world states. They have been shown to outperform action-only models across various robotic manipulation tasks. How- ever, representing the future with full-frame video prediction can be computation- ally expensive during both training and inference. This raises a central question: what compact state representation preserves the planning and supervision bene- fits of future prediction? In this paper, we propose BoxWAM, which replaces dense future frames with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant ob- jects. By explicitly imagining object-centric future motion, our method provides a lightweight prediction target that captures the key physical changes induced by robot actions. We show that box trajectory prediction substantially reduces com- putational cost while improving action prediction performance, suggesting that object-centric compact states can serve as an efficient alternative to video-based world action modeling for robotic manipulation. Result videos can be found on https://box-wam.github.io

title: Recovery of Rough Sources in the Inverse Monge--Ampère Problem
authors: Gunther Uhlmann, Philipp Zimmermann
abstract: We prove that every nonnegative source \(f\in L^1(Ω)\) in the Monge--Ampère equation \[ \det D^2u=f\quad\text{in }Ω, \] on a bounded uniformly convex \(C^{1,1}\) domain \(Ω\subset\mathbb R^n\), \(n\geq2\), is uniquely determined by generalized boundary measurements of Alexandrov solutions. The measurement is the extremal boundary slope, which extends the outward normal derivative and may equal \(+\infty\). For each \(ω\in\mathbb S^{n-1}\), it suffices to know these slopes for the cylindrical Dirichlet data \[ \frac{t_k^ω}{2}|P_ωx|^2,\qquad t_k^ω\to\infty, \] along any sequence of amplitudes, where \(P_ω\) projects onto \(ω^\perp\). The boundary value and extremal slope determine the interior subgradient image up to a Lebesgue null set. An exact change-of-variables formula and a large-amplitude limit then recover the Euclidean X-ray transform of \(f\), yielding uniqueness without a positive lower bound on the source. For nonnegative \(L^\infty\) sources, the extremal slopes are bounded and coincide with the interior normal derivatives, giving a Dirichlet-to-interior-Neumann formulation. The argument also extends to \[ \vartheta(\nabla u)\det D^2u=f, \] where the known weight \(\vartheta\) is locally integrable, Borel measurable, and bounded below by a positive constant. Conditional on existence of the corresponding Alexandrov solutions, the same cylindrical boundary-slope data determine every nonnegative \(L^1\) source.

title: An Optimal Algorithm for Changing from Longitudinal to Latitudinal Formation of Autonomous Aircraft Squadrons
authors: Paulo André Sperandio Giacomin, Elder Moreira Hemerly
abstract: This work presents an algorithm for changing from longitudinal to latitudinal formation of autonomous aircraft squadrons. The maneuvers are defined dynamically by using a predefined set of 3D basic maneuvers. This formation change is necessary when the squadron has to perform tasks demanding both formations, such as landing, lift-off, obstacle avoidance and georeferencing. The time complexity analysis of the transformation algorithm reveals that its efficiency is optimal. Simulations show that the formation change is done without collision, and the proof of correctness ensures its latitudinal formation features.

title: Rethinking World Models for Biosignals
authors: Xianglong Bao, Bosong Huang, Xiaoda Wang, Keqi Han, Carl Yang, Ming Jin, Shirui Pan
abstract: World models promise to learn how systems evolve and respond to actions, enabling simulation, planning and decision-making. Bringing this promise to biosignals requires more than accurate prediction of physiological recordings. We examine existing biosignal world models through two requirements for intervention use: a genuine action and evidence of its causal effect. We identify three fundamental bottlenecks rooted in physiology: Temporal Latency, the variable delay between an action and its observable effect; System Openness, the influence of drivers beyond the modelled intervention; and Endogenous Dynamics, the system's ongoing evolution without that intervention. Drawing on published evidence, we outline corresponding research directions and propose an Intervention-Effect Validation Checklist to guide evaluation. The aim is to help the biosignal community realise the core promise of world models by learning the latent mechanisms that govern physiological evolution and responses to interventions.

title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo State Networks
authors: Polyphony Bruna, Rick Dale, Michael J. Spivey, Christopher T. Kello
abstract: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.

title: Photoacoustic imaging of human brain function through intact adult skulls
authors: Yilin Luo, Rui Cao, Manxiu Cui, Karteekeya Sastry, Kay Jann, Yousuf Aborahama, Geng Ku, Jinhua Xu, Xiaofei Luo, Shuai Na, Samuel Davis, Konstantin Maslov, Yang Zhang, Danny J. Wang, Lihong V. Wang
abstract: Blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has revolutionized noninvasive imaging of human brain function, but it indirectly senses deoxyhemoglobin through water-proton relaxation and relies on bulky, costly, noisy, enclosed, superconducting-magnet scanners. In contrast, photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) directly probes hemoglobin absorption using a more compact, lower-cost, quieter, open, magnet-free system. However, functional PACT of the adult human brain has so far been demonstrated only after surgical skull removal, because the skull strongly attenuates optical and acoustic signals. Here, we demonstrate non-invasive transcranial functional PACT (T-fPACT) through the intact adult skull. A densely packed, high-channel-count (3,072-element) hemispherical ultrasonic array provides near-$2π$-steradian simultaneous acquisition, enabling high sensitivity and single-shot three-dimensional imaging at 20 Hz that eliminates motion blurring. Participant-specific stabilization further enables measurement of small task-evoked hemodynamic responses over the entire task duration. In healthy adults, T-fPACT localized responses to expected sensorimotor regions, distinguished task-specific motor representations, and yielded consistent localizations across repeated task runs and visits. Comparison with high-field (7 T) fMRI showed spatially corresponding functional regions, while dual-wavelength imaging revealed distinct hemoglobin-weighted responses. These findings overcome the long-standing skull barrier in human brain PACT and establish non-invasive, rapid volumetric photoacoustic imaging of brain function.

title: Two-level additive Schwarz preconditioners with GDSW coarse spaces for high-order discretizations in 2D
authors: Tommaso Bevilacqua, Axel Klawonn, Martin Lanser, Adam Wasiak
abstract: Two-level overlapping Schwarz preconditioners with Generalized Dryja-Smith-Widlund (GDSW) and Reduced GDSW (RGDSW) coarse spaces for high-order finite element methods (FEM) and virtual element methods (VEM) are investigated and applied to the Poisson problem in 2D. The GDSW coarse space is a well-established robust choice for preconditioners in domain decomposition, while the RGDSW coarse space offers a competitive alternative by reducing the coarse problem dimension while maintaining robustness. On the theoretical side, a condition number bound for both preconditioners is proved for conforming $\mathbb{P}_k$ and $\mathbb{Q}_k$ finite element spaces with explicit dependence on the polynomial degree $k$. Through numerical experiments on structured triangular and quadrilateral meshes for FEM and on polygonal meshes for VEM, it is demonstrated that both GDSW and RGDSW maintain scalability properties across polynomial orders up to $k=9$ for selected degrees. The RGDSW approach achieves a reduction in the coarse problem dimension by a factor of approximately three compared to GDSW while maintaining competitive iteration counts.

title: Dynamical BEC formation and vanishing entropy for trapped bosons in non-relativistic QED via nonlinear resonance cascades
authors: Thomas Chen, Ali Mezher
abstract: The dynamical formation of a complete Bose-Einstein condensate and the asymptotic purification of trapped bosons coupled to a quantized radiation field are rigorously established. By tracking the macroscopic one-particle density matrix $κ_T$ through a nonlinear resonance cascade, it is demonstrated that radiative relaxation irreversibly depletes all excited trap modes, even when the initial macroscopic state $κ_0$ is genuinely mixed. Here $κ_T$ is an average, with respect to a de Finetti measure $μ_0$, over mean-field particle-field orbits, so that the mixedness of $κ_0$ reflects a statistical ensemble of orbits. Under the assumptions of a non-vanishing initial ground state component and strictly positive downward Fermi-Golden-Rule rates, strong trace-norm convergence to a pure condensate is proven, $$ \lim_{T\to\infty} \| κ_T-|χ_0\rangle\langleχ_0| \|_{\mathfrak{S}_1(\mathfrak{h})} = 0 \, . $$ Furthermore, the von Neumann entropy of the macroscopic one-particle density matrix is shown to vanish asymptotically, $$ \lim_{T\to\infty}S[κ_T]=0 \, , $$ without any claim of monotonicity in $T$. Thus, any initially mixed, positive-entropy state ($0<S[κ_0]<\infty$) is purified to the ground state $|χ_0\rangle\langleχ_0|$. For the proof, we derive the Hartree hierarchy of the coupled system of bosons and photons from the finite-$N$ BBGKY hierarchy of the microscopic quantum many-body system, establishing trace-norm convergence in the mean-field limit as $N\to\infty$. The limits are taken successively; first $N\to\infty$, then the weak-coupling limit, and finally $T\to\infty$. Although the global particle-field evolution remains unitary, the macroscopic one-particle state converges to a pure state as energy and correlations are continuously radiated into the dispersive field.

title: Generic boundary behavior of Dirichlet eigenfunctions
authors: Alec Payne, Zihui Zhao
abstract: We extend Uhlenbeck's classical results on the generic properties of Laplacian eigenfunctions. In particular, we find a residual set of $C^k$ domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$, $k > n$, such that the nodal set of any Dirichlet eigenfunction intersects the boundary orthogonally along a $C^{k-1}$ embedded submanifold, whenever the intersection is non-empty. This is achieved by analyzing the boundary asymptotics of Dirichlet eigenfunctions via homogeneous harmonic polynomials and comparing their respective nodal sets. Along the way, we give a complete proof that generic Euclidean domains have simple Dirichlet eigenfunctions with zero as a regular value in the interior and zero as a regular value of the boundary normal derivative. In the special case of planar domains, a different argument provides one-parameter families of perturbed domains with the desired properties.

title: Nudge the Judge: Uncovering Program Decision Hijacking in Real-World Jev Applications
authors: Yang Luo, Tiantian Ji, Zifeng Kang, Yucheng Wang, Yong Liu, Zhiyi Yin, Xinran Liu
abstract: System One models such as Jev change how software makes decisions by mapping open-ended semantic contexts into structured judgments that directly drive program execution. However, this paradigm introduces a new security risk, which we term Jev Program Decision Hijacking (JPDH): attacker-controlled contexts can redirect program decisions through schema-valid Jev judgments. Existing evaluations focus primarily on model-level attacks or predefined injection channels, leaving attack reachability and downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications underexplored. In this paper, we present JevProbe, the first automated framework to evaluate JPDH by tracing adversarial influence from reachable context surfaces through program-consumed decisions to downstream security consequences in real-world Jev applications. Our key insight is that application logic maps diverse Jev judgments to observable decisions, enabling systematic, program-grounded attack evaluation. Across 228 popular real-world Jev applications and 2,273 test cases, 81.5% exhibit decision flips, of which 98.6% lead to potential downstream security impacts. Compared with the strongest adapted baseline, JevProbe improves macro-average Decision Flip Rate (DFR) by 50.4 percentage points, while existing defenses offer limited protection. We further construct JevProbeBench to support systematic evaluation of JPDH in real-world Jev applications. We have responsibly disclosed our findings to Jev application maintainers, pending their responses. The source code of JevProbe and the JevProbeBench dataset are publicly available on GitHub (https://github.com/xiaoxiaohg8d/JevProbe-).

title: Beyond the Encoder: Object-Centric Representations Emerging from Segmentation Foundation Models
authors: Michalis Pistos, Bartłomiej W. Papież
abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used as feature extractors for downstream tasks with limited data, typically through representations obtained from their encoders. However, foundation models trained for structured tasks such as segmentation also form object-specific representations during task execution, whose transferability remains largely unexplored. We investigate Segment Anything Model 2 (SAM2) object pointers, compact object-level representations produced through the segmentation pathway, as transferable representations for downstream tumour prediction. Through experiments on two PET/CT tumour prediction tasks, we find that object pointers learned using segmentation supervision alone already encode tumour-discriminative information, despite never being optimised for the downstream labels. We further introduce task-guided object pointers, where an auxiliary objective jointly shapes the object pointer space for the downstream prediction together with segmentation. Task-guided pointers improve cancer-type classification, outperforming conventional encoder-based transfer and radiomics, while segmentation-only pointers perform best on the more challenging recurrence prediction task. Representation analyses reveal associations between object pointers and interpretable radiomics features, class-dependent organisation of the learned representation space, and explicit spatial grounding around the segmented tumour. Together, these findings suggest that useful transferable representations can emerge through the execution of a foundation model's primary task, providing an alternative to conventional encoder-based transfer.

title: HULK: An Efficient Algorithm for Enabling Fast Bulk Bitwise Operations on Homomorphically Encrypted Data
authors: Mayank Kabra, Phillip Widdowson, Harshita Gupta, Rakesh Nadig, Nisa Bostancı, Eirini Tzermpou, Rakesh Kumar, Spiros Galanopoulos, Ataberk Olgun, Abdullah Giray Yağlıkçı, Mohammad Sadrosadati, Onur Mutlu
abstract: A wide range of important cloud applications, e.g., database analytics, graph analytics, and genome analysis, spend a considerable amount of time performing bulk bitwise operations (e.g., AND, OR, XOR). These applications often operate on highly sensitive data, making data privacy a critical concern. Homomorphic encryption (HE) enables secure computation on encrypted data without requiring decryption, ensuring privacy in untrusted and shared environments. We analyze 13 end-to-end applications across three domains (healthcare, graph, and database analytics) and observe that bulk bitwise operations take 62-100% of the execution time of the healthcare and graph workloads. The key problem is that existing HE approaches perform them with high-latency homomorphic operations (e.g., multiplication or lookup tables) and significantly increase the data size. Our goal is to enable fast bulk bitwise operations on homomorphically encrypted data by designing an efficient HE algorithm that reduces the use of these costly operations. To this end, we propose HULK, which performs two key steps: (1) it constructs bulk bitwise operations using low-cost homomorphic additions, which compute the Hamming weight of the encrypted operand bits in every slot of a packed ciphertext without any homomorphic multiplication, and (2) it decodes the result of an AND, OR, or XOR from the Hamming weight with a single indicator polynomial, keeping the result in the standard encoding. Across 13 end-to-end applications in healthcare, graph, and database analytics, HULK improves performance over the arithmetic approach used by prior works by up to 7.26x (CPU) and 6.65x (GPU), and on average by 2.32x/1.78x/1.45x (CPU) and 2.08x/1.70x/1.51x (GPU) for healthcare/graph/database analytics. When we increase the reduction depth in a representative application, HULK's speedup grows to 10.10x over the state-of-the-art GPU baseline.

title: Agentic4PDM: Host-Governed Evidence Admissibility for Industrial Fault Diagnosis
authors: Nam V. Nguyen, Hoang Van Truong, Hieu D. D., Duy Khuong Nguyen, Quang Pham, Tung Kieu
abstract: We study industrial fault diagnosis as a classification task that assigns sensor time-series windows to predefined health states or fault types. Scarce labels and changing operating conditions make repeated training of specialized classifiers costly. Yet structures such as periodicity, trends, and transients can remain diagnostically informative and be examined through reusable analytical tools. LLM agents can select and interpret these tools, but fixed rules or training-derived guidance may not resolve each signal's ambiguity, while unconstrained interpretation may overstate weak or conflicting results. We introduce Agentic4PDM, a framework that separates adaptive investigation from control over evidence use. LLM agents compare each signal with labeled references from every candidate class, identify unresolved distinctions, and propose follow-up measurements. A deterministic software controller, called the host, enforces contract-checked gated adjudication (CCGA): it checks requests, requires commitment to a complete tool batch before results are observed, and assigns evidence roles based on tool checks against labeled references. These roles distinguish corroborative support from advisory information. The Judge Agent proposes a diagnosis, while the controller checks protocol compliance and records the investigation. Agentic4PDM supports training-free diagnosis using pretrained representations and labeled references without task-specific diagnostic models, and a standard setting that additionally investigates trained-model predictions. Experiments on selected bearing and motor diagnosis challenges and an unfiltered industrial test set supplied by our customer show gains in aggregate macro F1 over the evaluated diagnostic and agentic baselines. Ablations further support the value of the governed workflow.

title: Stably exotic knotted surfaces up to equivalence
authors: Daniel Galvin, Daniel Kasprowski
abstract: In this short note we show the existence of stably exotic knotted surfaces in 4-manifolds in the sense that the embedded surfaces are topologically equivalent but are not smoothly equivalent even after any number of internal and external stabilisations.

title: Directed percolation in higher-order social dilemmas
authors: Pablo Villegas, Sandro Meloni
abstract: Multiplayer social dilemmas on hypergraphs show a variety of emergent phenomena, which has been attributed to group interactions. Here we test whether pairwise dynamics can reproduce them as well. We derive the mesoscopic Langevin equation of a testbed model and find the operator content of absorbing phase transitions: a directed-percolation line, a tricritical point, and a first-order region whose spinodal is the explosive transition. In our analysis, three-player games only set the values of the Landau coefficients. We construct a strictly pairwise model with short-lived memory, in which every event involves at most two entities, that reproduces these coefficients term by term and has exactly the same mean-field fixed points. Simulations confirm that the two dynamics share mean-field critical and tricritical scaling and the size of the critical mass, and that a purely three-player game on a two-dimensional triangular lattice lies in the directed-percolation class. For these games, the explosive transition and the critical mass therefore do not require group interactions, and the critical behavior is that of the pairwise theory.

title: Unsupervised and Supervised Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 2)
authors: Thierry Bouwmans, Anastasia Zakharova, Belmar Garcia, Marwa Chendeb El Rai, Meghna Kapoor, Badri Narayan Subudhi
abstract: Since the rise of supervised deep learning modelet dets, researchers has attempt to solve infrared small targection using various models like conventional neural networks, GANS, Transformers, Mixture of Experts and recent graph/hypergraph neural networks. Moreover, these deep neural networks methods surpassed the traditional unsupervised models and the low-rank and sparse decomposition unsupervised models reviewed in "Traditional and Recent Approaches for Infrared Small Target Detection : Overview, Challenges and Perspectives (Part 1). In this context, the aim of this paper is to provide a complete survey of the deep learning models in infrared small target detection. First, we categorize the different approaches found in the literature in terms of the modeling models of strategies. Then, we have discussed them in terms of the critical situations that they claim to handle. Furthermore, we present the specific performance evaluation. Then, we conclude with several promising directions for future research.

title: Role of dissipation dilution in achieving high mechanical quality factors in van der Waals resonators
authors: Lukas Schleicher, Leonard Geilen, Alexander Musta, Niklas Walter, Anne Rodriguez, Philipp Bredol, Alexander W. Holleitner, Eva M. Weig
abstract: Dissipation dilution has driven a revolution in the quality factors ($Q$) of top-down nanomechanical resonators. Yet it has not been leveraged for van der Waals (vdW) materials. Here we report quality factors up to $372{,}000\pm37{,}000$ in monolayer MoS$_2$ drums at 4 K, nearly an order of magnitude beyond the previous best for any vdW material at this temperature, enabled by a clean, polymer-free exfoliation technique. We develop a dissipation-dilution model for circular drums and analyze the contributing intrinsic and extrinsic dissipation mechanisms. The MoS$_2$ monolayer exhibits a dilution factor of order $1,000$, establishing sub-nanometer-thin resonators as ultimate dilution materials. The intrinsic quality factor, however, is limited by surface losses at atomic thickness. Conversely, multilayer drums show a lower dilution factor but a high intrinsic quality factor, on par with established top-down materials of similar dimensions, both resulting from the increased thickness. A two-level-system analysis of the temperature-dependent damping confirms this bulk-versus-surface picture and provides first insight into its microscopic origin. Our results identify dissipation dilution as the governing mechanism for high-$Q$ mechanical vdW resonators. Combined with strategies such as soft clamping or stress engineering, they establish atomically thin resonators as a platform for ultrahigh-$Q$ quantum transduction and sensing.
